subject: Computer Networking
title: Top-of-Rack Switches
description: Learn Top-of-Rack Switches in one minute.

hook.text: In a data center, every server rack has its own switch at the top. It's called a ToR switch.

buildup.text: Servers connect to the ToR with short copper cables. The ToR uplinks to the fabric with fiber.

discovery.text: ToR switches keep most traffic local. Server-to-server within a rack never leaves the switch.

twist.text: White-box switches run open-source OS like SONiC. Google and Facebook build their own, skipping Cisco.

climax.text: A single ToR handles 25-100 Gbps per server port and 400 Gbps uplinks. Enormous throughput.

punchline.text: The ToR switch is every server's first hop. Speed starts here.

quiz.question: Why are top-of-rack switches placed in each server rack?
options: To keep local server traffic within the rack and reduce latency
To provide wireless access to the data center
To convert AC power to DC for the servers

details.summary: Top-of-rack switches sit at the top of each server rack in a data center, connecting all servers in that rack to the network fabric. They minimize cable runs by providing 10 to 100 Gbps server connections locally while using high-speed uplinks to connect to the spine layer.
details.whyItMatters: Top-of-rack design is the dominant data center networking model. It simplifies cabling, improves airflow, and standardizes how servers connect to the network fabric.
takeaways: ToR switches connect all servers in a rack with short cables
High-speed uplinks connect each ToR to the spine layer
This design minimizes cross-rack cable runs and complexity

faq.question: How many servers does a top-of-rack switch connect?
faq.answer: A typical 1U ToR switch has 48 server-facing ports at 10 or 25 Gbps and 4 to 8 uplink ports at 40 or 100 Gbps. This connects up to 48 servers per rack. High-density configurations use two ToR switches per rack for redundancy.

faq.question: What is the alternative to top-of-rack?
faq.answer: End-of-row places larger switches at the end of each row serving multiple racks. Middle-of-row centers the switch between racks. These designs use longer server cables but require fewer switches overall. Top-of-rack dominates because shorter cables are more reliable and airflow-friendly.
